newsitem.title: USA: US IPOs seen finicky after spring fever.
newsitem.headline: US IPOs seen finicky after spring fever.

text.p: The speculative fervor that drove initial public offerings into orbit and raised nearly $50 billion in 1996 has faded, leaving a more conservative approach that means fewer, but higher quality deals for 1997.

In the spring, IPOs soared to astronomical levels, raising record levels of cash. For the year, 868 new offerings raised $49.9 billion, outpacing the 709 deals that raised $41.7 billion in 1993, according to Securities Data Corp.
"We're not going to see another time with a million deals going public and so many getting pushed through," said Linda Intini, vice president at Citibank Global Asset Management.
Buyers drove up stocks of early-stage firms with no history of profits early in the year. The average first-day gain of an IPO in April and May was 25 percent, Securities Data said.
Underwriters profited from the frenzy, raking in $3.5 billion, or 7 percent of the total cash raised.
"There was a period earlier this year when you could throw almost any IPO and it would stick," said David Bayer, portfolio manager at American Express Financial Advisers.
"But it was only a teaser" said Intini. IPO buyers were in for a nasty surprise.

The mood was souring as an Achilles heel began to show. Many fledgling companies were posting weak earnings or losses. And on July 5, a broad market sell-off doused IPOs as investors fled to the safety and liquidity of blue chips.
Even high-flying deals suffered. Internet browser Yahoo! Inc. rocketed 154 percent at its debut and peaked at $43 but now trades around $18, close to its $13 IPO price.
"Investors are looking at their portfolios at the end of the year and seeing a lot of broken deals in there," Intini said.
"Broken" deals are those that fall below their IPO price.
The earlier furious pace of 1996 meant a stampede of companies to Wall Street, leaving choosy investors looking at a field of slim pickings for 1997.
"The pipeline is really drained for next year so I expect less filing volume," said Bayer.

"Quality has been deteriorating. ... With so many IPOs, we ran a lot of industry leaders through. ... Now they are coming public earlier and earlier in the business cycle. It shows as a deterioration in balance sheets," said Matt Considine, portfolio manager of the Phoenix Mid Cap Fund.
Considine said fund managers were in a much better position than earlier this year to dictate prices.

"In the last six months of 1996, institutional buyers began shying away from 'concept' stocks with no revenues or earnings and negative cash flow. ... We don't see that changing," said Marc Paley, the head of the syndicate desk at Lehman Brothers.
The technology sector is likely to show promise in 1997, analysts agreed.

"We may get renewed interest in techs as we figure out how to make money on the Internet. We will find out who will make money and who will be providing the transactions. It could happen in the second half of 1997 or later," said Intini.
The growing number of global companies seeking U.S. listings could also drive volume.

Paley said, "We had Lucent (Technologies Inc.), Deutsche Telekom (AG), CANTV, and Telefonica del Peru (SA). A preponderance of those kinds of deals will drive volume for 1997. I think the privatisation trend out of Asia, Europe and Latin America will continue."

Other sectors mentioned as 1997 performers: biotechnology, medical devices, energy companies, and cyclical stocks. And new trends will likely emerge, much like the cigar trend this year and microbreweries in 1995.

But although IPOs are no longer shooting the moon, the market is still quite healthy albeit quieter. The fourth quarter was the second strongest quarter ever, Securities Data said, with 256 issues raising $14.6 billion, second only to the second quarter of 1996.
"As long as the fund flows are there to support them," there are still healthy numbers ahead, Phoenix Mid Cap's Considine said.
